Is anyone a hundred percent on your side?

sections.title: What being on your side actually looks like

blocks.p: This one starts with a question from someone in my community. We'd been focusing on co-regulation, and on self-regulation leading to co-regulation, and this person wrote:

q: I have hurt people who I'm close to with my defensiveness in my unregulated state, which makes it hard for them to co-regulate with me. Distancing further from them and seeking out those who can be a hundred percent for me without having any needs of their own seems like a risky path.

blocks.p: If I can sum it up: they've hurt somebody, or several people, from their dysregulated, traumatized state, and that makes it hard for those people to co-regulate with them. And distancing further from them and finding other people who are more trustworthy seems difficult, or risky. Yes, of course it is.
This brings a number of things to mind for me: co-regulation, repairing relationships, regret, trust, and vulnerability. I'll take them one by one.

Co-regulation is not just supporting each other and listening to each other. It's a neurobiological communication happening between two mammals. That's the nerdy way to put it. Basically, we send signals to each other that help each other feel better.

It's the giving and receiving of safety cues, or at least the giving of them. Another person, or another mammal, who's in more of a defensive state receives those cues, and ideally they help that person get into their own safety state. But it doesn't always go that easily.

So if you've hurt people, if you've wronged someone in your life, they're probably not going to be able to send you cues of safety. They're not going to be able to send you warm and fuzzies. That's not going to happen, and it's not realistic to expect it.
Two things can get in the way of co-regulation.
A rupture. Say you're hanging out with somebody, chit-chatting, and they stop and look at their phone. That's a rupture, and it's really easy to repair.

Misattunement. This is when you and the person you're communicating with are in different states. You might be in a flight and fight sympathetic state, and the other person is in a dorsal vagal shutdown state. The person in flight and fight has a lot more energy in their system. The person in shutdown lacks energy. That's misattunement.

To repair a rupture, it's pretty simple. You might just apologize: "My bad." You can smile, give eye crinkles, get back on track, and listen to that person. That's usually enough. It's not that complex.

Basically: acknowledge the hurt, empathize, listen, and give them some space if needed. If you really hurt that person and they need space, that's fine. If it's something more serious, giving them a little time on their own might be part of repairing the rupture.

When you're in different states, the other person might need more space for a longer period of time, and that's okay. Someone in shutdown does well when they're alone. They kind of need quiet and lower stimulation. Someone in flight and fight might also need a lot of space. So giving that person space can help repair misattunement.

The other thing you can do is self-regulate. Access your own safety state, so that when you do interact with that other person, you're offering them safety cues and really starting the process of co-regulation. If that happens, the other person is more likely to be able to access their safety state from your safety cues.

blocks.h: If you've hurt someone, the repair starts with you

blocks.p: Back to the question. It's not realistic to expect co-regulation from somebody you have flat-out hurt or flat-out wronged. That person probably isn't going to be able to provide you with adequate co-regulation. They're probably, rightfully, in a defensive state. Not just upset, but in more of a flight and fight state because of your actions.

So the onus is really on you to repair that relationship: to repair the rupture, to self-regulate, to offer them co-regulation, and hopefully to repair the misattunement. It's up to you to begin that process. It's really not up to them to do it for you.
They might be in a position where they can self-regulate through it and offer to reconnect with you. That might happen.

blocks.h3: When you're the one who was hurt

blocks.p: You might actually be on the other side of this. Somebody wronged you in some way. They hurt you, and it's valid and normal that you feel that way. They may not be the one to start the process of healing or repairing the relationship, and that might fall on you. Maybe you're not ready for that, and that's fine. But maybe you are.

That's pretty darn common in my time as a therapist. A lot of times, the people in my clients' lives need therapy a lot more than they do, but they're not getting it. So the person in therapy is actually the one in a better position to begin to self-regulate and to begin to heal that relationship. It doesn't mean the other person is open to it. But the one who was wronged or hurt might be the one to start the process of repair, sadly.

That might be true for you. It might be part of your journey of healing, but that's totally up to you and what you want to do with it. Ideally, though, I believe the one who has hurt another is the one to initiate some sort of repair.

blocks.h: Do you repair, or do you move on?

blocks.p: So if the person you've harmed can't provide you co-regulation, if they can't self-regulate and offer connection to you, do you abandon them and try to find it somewhere else? It depends. I think the answer is maybe. Or maybe not.

Maybe you've created that much of a rupture and that much of a lasting misattunement that it's irreparable. I think that's pretty common in severe childhood abuse and neglect, and in extreme situations like kidnapping and torture. If you have CPTSD, the parent or caregiver who was supposed to be good enough for you wasn't. There may be something irreparable there for you, and I don't think it's up to you to repair it.

So do you move on from somebody who isn't able to provide you co-regulation? If you've done something that heinous, and they're not willing to repair it with you, then yeah, maybe you do move on, and find connection and trust and co-regulation somewhere else.
But also, maybe not. Maybe you do apologize. Maybe you do make amends. Maybe you do try to make it better.

blocks.h3: Make your attempts, then accept the answer

blocks.p: I don't think repair has to be a process that goes on forever. You can definitely make your attempts, especially after you've self-regulated. But if that person isn't willing to accept it, that's their choice. You can't force it on someone. So offer up your attempts, and if they're batted away repeatedly, you've gotten your answer.

The other thing that might happen is that when you offer to make things better, the other person takes advantage of that. If they're asking you to do something that sacrifices your values, your morals, or your dignity, I think it's okay to say no.

Basically, you do the best you can. If it's a no, it's a no. Eventually, after repeated no's, it's out of your hands, and I think you need to take solace in the fact that you tried, even though you may have lost the relationship. If you can honestly say you've done the best you can to work on yourself and offered to work on the relationship, there's something to that.

So maybe you try to fix it. Maybe you don't. Maybe you try to make it better, but you have a boundary you won't cross: you won't violate your own morals, your values, or your dignity. I think that's fine too.

blocks.h: Regret and guilt are telling you something

blocks.p: When it comes to relationships where you've hurt someone and left a lasting impact, if you have regret, if you have guilt, that's a good thing. Those emotions are there for a reason. They're telling you that you harmed somebody, that you did something wrong. That's a healthy response. It shows you have empathy. It shows that you care.

If you were to harm somebody and not feel guilty, not feel regret, that's more of a red flag for me. So listen to it. Use that regret and that guilt as motivation to reach out, to apologize, to try to make a repair in the relationship.

Of course, guilt can also be imposed on you by someone else. It feels like guilt, but it's not because you did something wrong. It's more of an unhealthy kind of guilt lingering in your system. That's something you'll have to take stock of.

blocks.h: Is anyone a hundred percent on your side?

blocks.p: The second part of the question is about seeking out others who can be a hundred percent for us. I don't know if that's a thing. I don't know if anyone has ever been a hundred percent on our side.

I think what this person is asking is: should I go look for people I can trust completely? Trust is earned. It's not something you find right away. It develops and builds over time. So "I'm going to go find someone I can trust, someone who's a hundred percent on my side" is not going to be a short journey.

Co-regulation by itself doesn't require that you trust the person. People tend to think of it as the moment of discussing something and supporting someone emotionally. That's what it can look like, but co-regulation is really micro-moments of exchanging safety with each other. A genuine smile, eye crinkles, using your eyebrows: these all say, "I'm in a safety state, and I can offer you safety." That doesn't require that you trust me. It requires that you pick up on my safety cues. Co-regulation happens in micro-moments of unconscious communication.

Over time, those little shared moments of safety can lead to an experience, an emotion, of trust. Repeated co-regulation, along with actions, can help lead to trust, to connection, to healthy attachments, and to healthier relationships.
Opening up to somebody and being vulnerable, yes, that requires trust, and that trust is built on co-regulation.

blocks.h3: What being on your side actually looks like

blocks.p: I don't think anyone is ever going to be a hundred percent for you, and I don't think we should expect that. Other people will always have their own needs and their own agendas.

Honestly, the people who are truly supportive and on our side can also be challenging. That support can look like them expecting us to do better. It doesn't mean they'll hold our hand while we self-destruct. It might mean they back off and say, "I can't be a part of this anymore." It could also mean pushing us to do better with our life, to make better choices, to challenge ourselves to grow. People who are supportive and loving can do those things. Trust doesn't necessarily look like agreement with whatever you want to do with your life.

Actually, I know it doesn't. I'm completely on my kids' side, but that doesn't mean I support all their choices. If they choose to not do well in school, that is not acceptable. I love them so much that I will not allow that to happen. They must do better in school. Failure is not an option. If I were spoiling my kids and wanted to be their friend, I'd probably let it slide, but that is not the standard in our household.
So does anyone ever have someone a hundred percent on their side? I don't think it looks the way one might think it does.

Back to the question one more time: I've hurt people, they can't provide co-regulation, should I seek somebody else out and try to find trust and co-regulation there? Maybe. Co-regulation is very needed. We need each other. But the place you start might be self-regulation: working on yourself first, without trying to get co-regulation from somebody else.

I'm kind of worried about the idea of "I burned these relationships, and now they can't co-regulate with me, so let me go find new relationships with people who are completely for me and on my side." I don't know if that's what this person meant, but that's where my mind goes with it. We can't just jump from relationship to relationship without working on ourselves first. We can't bring the best version of ourselves to a new relationship unless we've developed it, unless we've worked on it.

I'm really worried about seeking out co-regulation from a dysregulated place, from desperation. If you're desperate for connection, and you may be fully entitled to be, there's no judgment here. But if you're looking for somebody else to make it better, to make you feel better, to fix your problems, that's probably not going to end up anywhere healthy. It might lead to more hurt for somebody else when they don't live up to what you want. And it could lead to you being hurt when someone exploits your desperation.

If you can self-regulate and access more of your polyvagal safety state, it's going to help a lot. It will help you make amends for the past, take ownership of what you've done, reach out to someone, offer apologies, and try to make things better, while holding strong boundaries and never sacrificing your values and your dignity. You'll be able to empathize with that person. You'll be able to act from compassion. As you build self-regulation, these things become options.
Self-regulation is not easy. It's a long process, and it doesn't happen overnight.
We all need co-regulation, but you might not have it in your life right now, and it is what it is. So you do the best you can, starting with self-regulation, and keep the rest really simple.

ol: Build an environment that feels safer than not. This is the first thing I recommend for building safety. If your home sets you up with passive safety cues, they provide a steady stream of safety. That's a foundation you can build off of, and once you have it, you can use more active self-regulation techniques.

Find safe and predictable avenues of connection. Connect with people who share your interests, if you can. Put a little more time into the relationships in your life where there's a little something there. That might be family, friends, acquaintances, coworkers, or professional co-regulation from a therapist.

Take connection where you can get it. Communicating in an online community, as text on a screen, isn't true co-regulation. Someone I was talking with called it virtual connection. It's not co-regulation, but it is a sense of connection, and that might be better than nothing.
Savor the co-regulation you do get. As you notice opportunities for co-regulation, really experience them mindfully. Or think back on them later in the day and try to experience them all over again.

blocks.p: Eventually, self-regulation might be where you need to go, and honestly, it might be the first step as well.
